messages.author: d54aba6af40f8c5e
messages.subject: Average Marginal Effect (AME)
parts:
Hello,

Using a simple model in INLA I can estimate the Average Marginal Effect (AME - average over empirical range of observed data) easily for a binary covariate x1=0,1.  (The continuous case is slightly more complicated). I simply create two copies of the original data, set the predicted outcome to NA, and set x1 to 0 in the first predicted dataset and x1 to 1 in the second.

I then use inla.predicted.sample as follows and get results that match up well when using the "margins" command (frequentist):

-------------------------------------------------------
require(margins)
require(INLA)

## simulation ##

set.seed(1)
N <- 1000
x1 <- sample(c(0,1),N,rep=T)
x2 <- rnorm(N)
mu <- 0.1 + 1.0*x1 + 0.5*x2 + 0.2*x1*x2
p <- plogis(mu)
y <- rbinom(N,1,prob=p)
dat <- data.frame(x1,x2,y)

## frequentist way

mod.glm <- glm(y ~ x1*x2,data=dat,family="binomial")
print( summary(margins(mod.glm)), digits=3)

## Bayesian way

pred.0 <- dat; pred.0$x1 <- 0; pred.0$y <- NA
pred.1 <- dat; pred.1$x1 <- 1; pred.1$y <- NA
dat.pred <- rbind(dat,pred.0,pred.1)

require(INLA)
mod.inla <- inla(y ~ x1*x2,family="binomial",data=dat.pred,
                 control.compute=list(config=TRUE),
                 control.predictor=list(link=1),
                 )
M <- 1000
samp <- inla.posterior.sample(M,mod.inla)
latents <- t(sapply(samp,function(x) x$latent[,1]))
preds <- plogis(latents)[,which(is.na(dat.pred$y))]

## calculate ame
p0 <- preds[,1:N]
p1 <- preds[,N + 1:N]
ame <- rowMeans(p1-p0)
print( quantile(ame,probs=c(0.5,0.025,0.975)), digits=3)

## relative risks - hard to get from frequentist logistic models
rr.1.0 <- rowMeans(p1/p0)
quantile(rr.2.1,probs=c(0.5,0.025,0.975))

-----------------------------------------

I'm curious if this is perhaps a slow/inefficient way to do this. In particular, is there a way to do it without using inla.posterior.sample?

Thanks,

John

messages.author: 3eab71733027a24a
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Average Marginal Effect (AME)
parts:
Hi

this is the easy way to get properties of some joint function of p0 and
p1. If you are willing to ignore their posterior dependence, you can
just compute these properties directly from their marginals, but I
guess you would not. As an alternative, you may assume the linear
predictors for p0 and p1, are joint Gaussian, you can extract (from
defining appropriate linear combinations) the correlation between these
two, and then you have the Gaussian copula. Then you can just sample
from a bivariate normal or do integration in 2d.


H

messages.author: 3eab71733027a24a
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Average Marginal Effect (AME)
parts:
inla.posterior.sample() does now offer the option num.threads, so if
you have a big problem/many samples, you can do the sampling in
parallel. I got a little various results wrt speedup, so for this
reason this variable is default to 1.

If the option is not there, just upgrade to the most recent testing
version

H

parts:
Thanks again for your help.

I've estimated p1-p0 on the log odds scale using the appropriate matrix with lincombs "inla.make.lincombs(Predictor=B)".  I've also done it using the linear predictor way "control.predictor=list(A=A,compute=TRUE,link=1)". 

However, I want the estimator on the response (plogis) scale. The estimator represents a sum of predictors (across dataset), so I can't just transform the sum at the end - I need to transform each element of the sum. I can't seem to figure out how to do this, even using "link=1" in "control.predictor".

John

--------------------

pred.0 <- dat; pred.0$x1 <- 0; pred.0$y <- NA
pred.1 <- dat; pred.1$x1 <- 1; pred.1$y <- NA
dat.pred <- rbind(dat,pred.0,pred.1)

vec.1 <- rep(NA,N)
vec.2 <- rep(-1/N,N)
vec.3 <- rep(1/N,N)
B <- t(as.matrix(c(vec.1,vec.2,vec.3)))

lcs <- inla.make.lincombs(Predictor=B)
mod.inla.simple <- inla(y ~ 1 + x1*x2,
                        family="binomial",
                        data=dat.pred,
                        lincomb=lcs,
                        control.inla=list(strategy="gaussian"),
                        control.predictor=list(link=1)
                        )

## Too late to transform - This is a sum of predictors all on log odds scale
mod.inla.simple$summary.lincomb.derived

For non-trivial and/or nonlinear predictions you can always use posterior sampling; see inla.posterior.sample. With that, you can evaluate whatever function you need, and compute the posterior mean and variance and quantiles based on the samples.

Finn

logit(p1) and logit(p0)

are bivariate normal and from this derive the posterior for p1/p0

I hope I'm not missing something obvious. However, perhaps the sampling approach is the way to go here.
